type_rationale: The paper derives a thermodynamically consistent stress-coupled Cahn-Hilliard formulation with finite elasto-plastic kinematics, implements it by FEM, and applies it to two-phase lithiation of a circular silicon nanowire.
must_cover: Multiplicative chemical-plastic-elastic deformation and quasi-static mechanical equilibrium
Single conserved normalized Li concentration as both lithiation and phase indicator
Free-energy-derived chemical potential and stress-coupled Cahn-Hilliard transport
COMSOL weak-form implementation and boundary conditions
Sharp inward-moving phase front, stress reversal, and plasticity effects
Constant interface-width validation and stated coupling limitation
key_numbers: Young's modulus 160 to 40 GPa; yield strength 1.5 GPa; hardening modulus 1.0 GPa
central_claims: The coupled phase-field/finite-plasticity model preserves a material interface length scale while resolving large deformation.
Late-stage surface tensile hoop stress emerges because the lithiated outer shell constrains expansion at the inward-moving front.
The computed stress fields are broadly consistent with a prior nonlinear concentration-dependent diffusion model.
claim_boundaries: The application is an idealized circular, isotropic nanowire under prescribed surface saturation and traction-free mechanics.
Plastic parameters are representative values fitted reasonably to experiments rather than directly measured for the modeled system.
A systematic kinetic study of stress feedback on diffusion and reaction is deferred.
mechanism_result_map: Double-well chemical energy plus gradient penalty -> stable Li-poor/Li-rich diffuse interface -> nearly constant 1.12 nm width.
Chemical swelling plus J2 plasticity -> redistribution and limiting of stresses -> early compression and late surface tension.
Variational chemical potential including elastic contribution -> stress-sensitive Li transport -> co-evolved concentration and geometry.
comparative_positioning: Unlike single-phase nonlinear diffusion, the phase-field formulation supplies an intrinsic interface thickness.
Unlike small-strain elastic phase-field models, it admits approximately 300% local volume expansion and plastic flow.
Stress-profile comparison uses the authors' prior nonlinear diffusion model rather than a new experimental field measurement.
negative_or_limiting_results: Small stress fluctuations remain in the phase-field solution, with mesh density, geometry, and plasticity law cited as possible causes.
The paper does not systematically quantify stress-induced retardation of transport or reaction kinetics.
The single concentration field collapses composition and crystalline/amorphous structure into one variable.
visual_plan: Figure 3 for inward migration and slowdown of the concentration front
Figure 4 for phase-field versus nonlinear-diffusion stress profiles
Figures 5-6 on page 8 for stress reversal/plasticity and interface-width validation
